Chapter 10 · Vibrations and the Debye heat capacity

Count vibrational modes in a solid and explain why a crystal’s low-temperature heat capacity follows a cube law.

From first principles

Derive the low-temperature heat capacity from acoustic modes

In a large three-dimensional crystal, long-wavelength acoustic vibrations have approximately linear dispersion \(\omega=vk\). Count allowed wavevectors inside a sphere of radius \(k\). Its volume grows as \(k^3\), so the number of modes below \(\omega\) grows as \(\omega^3\). The frequency density is its derivative. In a single-speed model normalized to the \(3N\) displacements of \(N\) atoms,

\[g(\omega)=\frac{9N\omega^2}{\omega_D^3},\]
\[\int_0^{\omega_D}g(\omega)\,d\omega=3N .\]

Each mode stores mean thermal energy \(\hbar\omega/[e^{\hbar\omega/(k_BT)}-1]\). Multiply by the mode count and substitute \(x=\hbar\omega/(k_BT)\) to expose the temperature dependence,

\[U_{\rm th}=\frac{9N(k_BT)^4}{\hbar^3\omega_D^3}\int_0^{\hbar\omega_D/(k_BT)}\frac{x^3}{e^x-1}\,dx .\]

When \(T\ll\hbar\omega_D/k_B\), the omitted tail above the upper limit is exponentially small. The integral approaches a constant, giving \(U_{\rm th}\propto T^4\) and \(C_V=(\partial U/\partial T)_V\propto T^3\). The cube law relies on both three-dimensional mode counting and linear low-frequency dispersion.

Derivation and applications

Recover the Debye velocity from distinct sound branches

A three-dimensional solid usually carries one longitudinal and two transverse acoustic polarizations. Their speeds can differ substantially. Consider a large elastically isotropic crystal of volume \(V\), with linear dispersion \(\omega=v_s k\) for each polarization \(s\) in the thermally populated range. Impose periodic boundaries; one wavevector state occupies reciprocal volume \((2\pi)^3/V\). For each polarization count all points in a sphere of radius \(\omega/v_s\), which includes opposite propagation directions. Differentiating gives the total density of modes,

\[N_s(<\omega)=\frac{V\omega^3}{6\pi^2v_s^3},\]
\[g(\omega)=\frac{V\omega^2}{2\pi^2}\left(v_L^{-3}+2v_T^{-3}\right).\]

A slower sound branch has more low-frequency states because the same frequency reaches a larger wavevector sphere. Define one effective velocity \(v_D\) to preserve this acoustic density of states. Requiring an isotropic monatomic Debye model to contain \(3N\) vibrations, with number density \(n=N/V\), fixes its frequency cutoff and temperature scale,

\[\frac{3}{v_D^3}=\frac{1}{v_L^3}+\frac{2}{v_T^3},\]
\[\omega_D=v_D(6\pi^2 n)^{1/3},\]
\[\Theta_D=\frac{\hbar\omega_D}{k_B}.\]

At low temperature the cutoff can be moved to infinity in the thermal energy integral. Changing variables to \(x=\hbar\omega/(k_BT)\) uses \(\int_0^\infty x^3/(e^x-1)\,dx=\pi^4/15\). A temperature derivative yields the directly measurable coefficient

\[\frac{C_V}{VT^3}=\frac{2\pi^2 k_B^4}{15\hbar^3}\left(v_L^{-3}+2v_T^{-3}\right).\]

The inverse cubes explain why replacing the three velocities by their arithmetic mean can noticeably underestimate the heat capacity. Optical or electronic contributions must be identified separately in specimens where they are thermally active.

Worked example

Predict the acoustic temperature scale

For \(v_L=6000\,\mathrm{m/s}\), \(v_T=3000\,\mathrm{m/s}\), the longitudinal branch contributes only \(1/17\) of the low-temperature coefficient. The effective velocity is

\[3000(24/17)^{1/3}=3365\,\mathrm{m/s}.\]

With \(n=5.00\times10^{28}\,\mathrm{m^{-3}}\), the cutoff wavevector is \(1.44\times10^{10}\,\mathrm{m^{-1}}\), giving \(\Theta_D\simeq369\,\mathrm K\). The long-wave estimates apply well below that scale.

Second application

Extract the transverse speed from calorimetry

Suppose a separate specimen gives \(v_D=2500\,\mathrm{m/s}\) from its low-temperature heat capacity and \(v_L=5000\,\mathrm{m/s}\) from a longitudinal pulse. Solving for the missing speed gives

\[v_T=[2/(3/v_D^3-1/v_L^3)]^{1/3}=2.22\times10^3\,\mathrm{m/s}.\]

A shear-wave transit across \(10.0\,\mathrm{mm}\) should consequently take \(4.51\,\mathrm{\mu s}\). This timing test uses a distinct mechanical measurement of the same states counted by calorimetry.

What a solid can store

Consider an electrically insulating three-dimensional crystal of \(N\) atoms, volume \(V\), sufficiently cold that its structure remains fixed and normal-mode frequencies vary weakly with temperature. In a harmonic approximation displacements about equilibrium separate into \(3N\) independent oscillators. Their excitations are called phonons. Phonon number is not conserved when the solid exchanges heat, so each mode has a Bose mean occupation with zero chemical potential. The modes exist because the crystal can deform, including at very long wavelengths.

A model assigning the same frequency to every oscillator predicts an exponentially small low-temperature heat capacity, since exciting any mode would require a fixed nonzero energy. Acoustic vibrations instead approach zero frequency as their wavenumber approaches zero. Even in a cold macroscopic crystal, long-wavelength modes can remain thermally accessible. The key quantity is how many have energies of order \(k_BT\) or less.

Test the single-frequency model before introducing a spectrum

The premise of the Einstein solid is deliberately restrictive. All \(3N\) vibrational coordinates of a crystal are independent harmonic oscillators with one frequency \(\omega_E\). For one coordinate the levels are \(E_n=\hbar\omega_E(n+1/2)\). Write \(x=\hbar\omega_E/(k_BT)=\Theta_E/T\). Summing the geometric series gives

\[Z_1=e^{-x/2}/(1-e^{-x}).\]

The partition function of the crystal is \(Z_1^{3N}\), because each normal coordinate can be occupied independently and phonon number is free to change.

Apply \(-\partial\ln Z/\partial\beta\), with \(\beta=1/(k_BT)\), to obtain

\[U=3N\hbar\omega_E[1/2+1/(e^x-1)].\]

The zero-point energy contributes no heat capacity at fixed volume. Differentiating the occupation term and using \(dx/dT=-x/T\) gives

\[C_{V,E}=3Nk_B\,\frac{x^2e^{-x}}{(1-e^{-x})^2}.\]

At high temperature \(1-e^{-x}\simeq x\), so the heat capacity per mole of atoms approaches \(3R\). At low temperature the denominator tends to one, and the surviving factor \(x^2e^{-x}\) measures the cost of the lowest available excitation. For \(\Theta_E=240\) K the same mole would have \(C_V=18.06\) J/(mol K) at 120 K, \(7.585\) at 60 K and \(0.536\) at 30 K. Halving temperature does not give a fixed ratio. The curve crosses from a classical plateau to thermally rare excitations.

A real three-dimensional macroscopic crystal supports collective vibrations whose frequencies approach zero with wavelength increasing. Replacing the single frequency by a distribution puts modes below any fixed nonzero thermal scale. The next calculation finds the density of those modes, and therefore a low-temperature power law. High-temperature agreement alone cannot distinguish the two models since both count the same total number of coordinates.

Practise on sheet 5 · Discriminate two low-temperature laws with a ratio. Further reading · University of Oxford · S. Simon, Lecture Notes for Solid State Physics · Chapter 2 · Specific Heat of Solids: Boltzmann, Einstein, and Debye · TUM / Walther-Meißner-Institut · R. Groß, Physik der kondensierten Materie I · §6.1.5 · Debye- und Einstein-Modell.

Count to a cutoff

Use a continuum approximation with three acoustic polarizations and a common sound speed \(v\). The modes in a shell of wavevectors grow as \(k^2dk\), as for photons. Real crystals generally have distinct longitudinal and transverse speeds. An effective Debye speed averages their inverse cubes. Converting via \(\omega=vk\) gives density \(g(\omega)=3V\omega^2/(2\pi^2v^3)\). The continuum would supply infinitely many modes, whereas a crystal with \(N\) atoms has exactly \(3N\). Choose an upper cutoff \(\omega_D\) to match that count,

\[\int_0^{\omega_D}g(\omega)\,d\omega=3N,\]
\[g(\omega)=9N\omega^2/\omega_D^3 .\]

This cutoff is an approximate representation of the lattice at high wavenumber. The low-temperature prediction depends on the long-wave acoustic spectrum and is insensitive to precise details near the cutoff. In a multi-atom cell additional optical branches change the intermediate-temperature behaviour, which cannot generally be reconstructed with a single effective speed.

Two limits and a measurement

The thermal energy is the integral of \(g(\omega)\hbar\omega/[\exp(\hbar\omega/k_BT)-1]\) over the band. Define \(\Theta_D=\hbar\omega_D/k_B\). When \(T\ll\Theta_D\), extend the upper limit of the dimensionless integral to infinity. The resulting energy scales as \(T^4\) and differentiation yields

\[C_V=\frac{12\pi^4}{5}Nk_B\left(\frac{T}{\Theta_D}\right)^3.\]

At high temperature each mode instead approaches \(k_BT\) of thermal energy and the heat capacity tends to \(3Nk_B\). The acoustic model has the correct count by construction. The constant zero-point energy never enters either heat capacity because it disappears upon differentiation.

For one mole of atoms with \(\Theta_D=300\) K, the low-temperature prediction at 10.0 K is \(0.0720\) J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, far below the classical \(3R=24.9\) J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. At 20.0 K the cubic asymptote predicts \(0.576\) J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. Measuring several temperatures and plotting \(C/T^3\) tests the constant coefficient directly. In a conducting solid an electronic term proportional to \(T\) can dominate at low temperatures. Separating that term through a plot of \(C/T\) against \(T^2\) allows the intercept and slope to reveal the two physically distinct energy stores.

Finite size eventually supplies a lower frequency cutoff related to the crystal dimensions, so the continuum counting argument presupposes a specimen large enough to have many wavelengths populated throughout the temperature interval.

Connect vibrations to thermal expansion

A purely harmonic crystal with force constants independent of volume can store vibrational energy yet has no vibrational mechanism for thermal expansion. Real vibrational frequencies usually vary as the lattice spacing changes. The quasiharmonic approximation treats each mode as harmonic at each volume while allowing its angular frequency \(\omega_j(V)\) to change smoothly. Define the mode Grüneisen parameter \(\gamma_j=-\partial\ln\omega_j/\partial\ln V\). A positive value means expansion softens that mode.

For one oscillator the Helmholtz free energy is

\[F_j=\hbar\omega_j/2+k_BT\ln[1-e^{-\hbar\omega_j/(k_BT)}].\]

Differentiation at fixed \(T\) gives

\[\partial F_j/\partial\omega_j=U_j/\omega_j,\]

where \(U_j\) includes the zero-point energy and the mean thermal excitation. Since vibrational pressure is \(-\partial F/\partial V\), the chain rule gives

\[p_{\rm vib}=V^{-1}\sum_j\gamma_j U_j.\]

A temperature derivative at fixed volume suppresses the constant zero-point contribution. The mechanical relation \((\partial p/\partial T)_V=\alpha_V B_T\) finally yields

\[\alpha_V=\frac{\sum_j\gamma_j C_{V,j}}{B_TV} .\]

Here \(B_T\) is the isothermal bulk modulus and \(\alpha_V\) the volume expansion coefficient. The mode sum weights each Grüneisen parameter by its thermally active heat capacity. A low-frequency mode that softens under compression can contribute negatively and can dominate in a cold crystal while high-frequency modes remain frozen. A single positive average parameter is therefore a material model rather than a thermodynamic necessity.

Infer a mode average from dilatometry

For a cubic crystal take measured molar heat capacity \(C_{V,m}=12.0\) J/(mol K), molar volume \(V_m=1.20\times10^{-5}\) m³/mol and bulk modulus \(B_T=100\) GPa. A measured linear expansion coefficient \(6.00\times10^{-6}\) K⁻¹ corresponds to \(\alpha_V\simeq3\alpha_L=1.80\times10^{-5}\) K⁻¹. The effective heat-capacity-weighted parameter is then

\[\bar\gamma=\alpha_VB_TV_m/C_{V,m}=1.80.\]

The factor of three comes from differentiating the cube of a length, not from counting acoustic polarizations again.

If the same positive average and bulk modulus remain approximately constant down to a regime where phonons give \(C_V\propto T^3\), the volume expansion coefficient should also fall as \(T^3\). Doubling temperature there increases the coefficient by about eight, although the accumulated length change requires integrating it over temperature. A comparison of \(\alpha_V/C_V\) at several temperatures can test whether the active modes really share a common volume sensitivity. Molar heat capacity and molar volume must be taken on the same chemical counting basis before inferring any dimensionless Grüneisen parameter.

Hydrostatic pressure spectroscopy gives an independent way to measure a mode parameter. By the chain rule, the definition yields \(\gamma_j=B_T(\partial\ln\omega_j/\partial p)_T\) within the quasiharmonic description. For the numerical bulk modulus, a mode with parameter 1.80 would increase its frequency by approximately 1.8 percent under a 1.00 GPa hydrostatic pressure increment. Agreement between this slope and the value inferred from expansion requires that the probed mode be representative of the thermally populated spectrum. A strong optical mode visible to a spectrometer need not dominate low-temperature heat capacity or expansion.

Quoted pressure derivatives must therefore specify the mode, the temperature and whether hydrostatic or directional stress was applied in the measurement.

Which lattice heat capacities survive at low temperature?

Compare a linear acoustic spectrum with a single oscillator frequency. Scale each temperature by its model’s characteristic temperature. The Debye prediction uses numerical quadrature of \(3t^3\int_0^{1/t}x^4e^x/(e^x-1)^2\,dx\); both expressions approach unity at high temperature.

A pressure thermometer and a calorimeter do not count molecular degrees of freedom in the same way. A dilute diatomic gas can retain nearly ideal pressure while its heat capacity changes appreciably as discrete internal levels become populated. Problem sheet 5 · Radiation and vibrations as mode gases

Connect equilibrium state counting to radiative transfer and distinguish a lattice heat capacity from electronic storage.

Two black surfaces

Two large parallel black surfaces at 350 K and 300 K face one another across vacuum. Calculate the net radiative flux. Linearize it about 325 K and assess the error. Use \(\sigma=5.6704\times10^{-8}\) W m⁻² K⁻⁴.

Show the transfer calculation

Net flux is

\[\sigma(350^4-300^4)=391.6\,\mathrm{W/m^2}.\]

The linear estimate \(4\sigma(325)^3(50)=389.3\) W/m² is about \(0.6\%\) low. For temperatures \(T_m\pm\Delta T/2\), expanding the fourth powers gives \(4T_m^3\Delta T+T_m(\Delta T)^3\). The omitted positive term explains the bias and shows how the relative error scales as \((\Delta T/T_m)^2\).

The missing calorimeter coefficient

Low-temperature molar measurements on a metal give \(C/T=4.00\) mJ mol⁻¹ K⁻² at 2.00 K and \(C/T=10.0\) mJ mol⁻¹ K⁻² at 4.00 K. Using \(C=\gamma T+\beta T^3\), extract both coefficients and the atomic Debye temperature. Take \(12\pi^4R/5=1944\) J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.

Show the separation of contributions

A plot of \(C/T\) against \(T^2\) has slope \(\beta=(10-4)/(16-4)=0.500\) mJ mol⁻¹ K⁻⁴ and intercept \(\gamma=4-0.5(4)=2.00\) mJ mol⁻¹ K⁻². From \(\beta=1944/\Theta_D^3\) obtain

\[\Theta_D=(1944/0.000500)^{1/3}=157\,\mathrm{K}.\]

The electronic term dominates below \(\sqrt{\gamma/\beta}=2.00\) K, provided the same low-temperature normal state persists.

Change the number of spatial dimensions

An idealized large sheet supports one acoustic branch with linear dispersion \(\omega=vk\) in two dimensions. Derive the low-temperature power of the thermal energy and heat capacity. Explain why a freely suspended membrane with a flexural branch may behave differently.

Show the mode count

The two-dimensional reciprocal-space annulus has area \(2\pi k\,dk\), hence \(g(\omega)\propto\omega\) for the linear branch. Integrating \(g(\omega)\hbar\omega/[e^{\hbar\omega/k_BT}-1]\) with \(x=\hbar\omega/k_BT\) gives

\[U_{\rm th}\propto T^3,\]
\[C\propto T^2.\]

A quadratic flexural branch instead gives \(k\,dk\) proportional to \(d\omega\), so the density of states is approximately constant and its contribution is proportional to \(T\) in heat capacity. The temperature exponent diagnoses both dimensionality and dispersion.

Discriminate two low-temperature laws with a ratio

A mole of insulating crystal is measured at fixed volume at 40 K and 20 K. The recorded lattice heat capacities are 0.800 and 0.101 J/(mol K). Compare their ratio with a Debye low-temperature prediction and with an Einstein model of \(\Theta_E=240\) K. Explain what conclusion these two readings support.

Worked solution

The measured ratio \(C_V(20)/C_V(40)=0.12625\) is close to the low-temperature acoustic prediction \((20/40)^3=0.125\). Applying the Einstein formula with \(x=6\) and \(12\) gives 2.237 and 0.02207 J/(mol K), a ratio of 0.00987. Even if one rescales its amplitude to match at 40 K, this proposed Einstein frequency predicts too sharp a fall.

The two measurements support an acoustic-mode contribution over this temperature interval. To establish the asymptotic exponent, take additional low-temperature measurements and examine \(C_V/T^3\), including uncertainty in both the calorimetry and the subtraction of electronic or background heat capacity. The ratio test alone supplies neither the whole phonon spectrum nor a unique microscopic model.

Chapter 11 · Chemical equilibrium and reaction extent

Minimize Gibbs energy along a permitted reaction and predict a composition change when the system is compressed.

From first principles

Build the reaction quotient from chemical potentials

At fixed temperature and pressure, a closed reacting mixture equilibrates by minimizing Gibbs energy subject to conservation of its constituent elements. Let \(\nu_i\) be the balanced stoichiometric coefficient of species \(i\), positive for a product and negative for a reactant. Advancing the reaction by a small extent \(d\xi\) changes each amount by \(dn_i=\nu_i d\xi\). The free-energy change per mole of reaction is then

\[\frac{dG}{d\xi}=\sum_i\nu_i\mu_i=\Delta_rG .\]

For an interior equilibrium this derivative vanishes. Chemical potentials can be written \(\mu_i=\mu_i^\circ+RT\ln a_i\) using dimensionless activities relative to specified standard states. Collecting all the logarithms gives

\[\Delta_rG=\Delta_rG^\circ+RT\ln Q,\]
\[Q=\prod_i a_i^{\nu_i},\]
\[K=e^{-\Delta_rG^\circ/(RT)}.\]

The equilibrium composition satisfies \(Q=K\). For an ideal gas, \(a_i=p_i/p^\circ\); nonideal mixtures require activities measured or modeled for the mixture. If \(Q<K\), a small forward reaction lowers \(G\). This thermodynamic preference determines a direction near the present state while leaving the reaction timescale to kinetics.

Background · Chemical potential
\[\mu=(\partial F/\partial N)_{T,V}\]

This change in free energy per added particle controls exchange between subsystems. In a finite small system an actual finite difference may matter.

Derivation and applications

Propagate an equilibrium constant when reaction heat capacity changes the enthalpy

An equilibrium constant quoted at one temperature does not determine the equilibrium composition at another unless the energy change of the reaction is also known. Consider a reversible reaction with a dimensionless standard equilibrium constant \(K(T)\) and unchanged standard-state choices. All reaction quantities below are per mole of reaction as written. At fixed standard pressure, the Gibbs differential \(dG=-S\,dT\), together with \(G=H-TS\), gives

\[d(G/T)/dT=-H/T^2.\]

Apply this identity to the stoichiometric differences of standard molar quantities,

\[\ln K=-\frac{\Delta_rG^\circ}{RT},\]
\[\frac{d\ln K}{dT}=\frac{\Delta_rH^\circ(T)}{RT^2}.\]

If heat capacities of products and reactants differ, the enthalpy changes with temperature. Over an interval where their stoichiometric difference \(\Delta_r C_p^\circ\) can be treated as constant, integration of \(dH^\circ=C_p^\circ dT\) gives

\[\Delta_rH^\circ(T)=\Delta_rH^\circ(T_1)+\Delta_r C_p^\circ(T-T_1).\]

Insert this linear enthalpy into the derivative for \(\ln K\). The constant part integrates as \(1/T^2\); the term proportional to temperature also produces a logarithm. The two-temperature relation is

\[\ln\frac{K_2}{K_1}=\frac{\Delta_rH^\circ(T_1)}{R}\left(\frac1{T_1}-\frac1{T_2}\right)+\frac{\Delta_r C_p^\circ}{R}\left[\ln\frac{T_2}{T_1}+\frac{T_1}{T_2}-1\right].\]

Both terms vanish when the two temperatures coincide. For a small temperature interval the heat-capacity correction begins at second order, consistent with the local slope depending only on the current reaction enthalpy. Phase changes would interrupt the assumed smooth enthalpy law.

Worked example

Estimate a change in an association equilibrium

Take \(K_1=4.00\) at \(300\,\mathrm K\), \(\Delta_rH^\circ(T_1)=-20.0\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}\), and \(\Delta_rC_p^\circ=100\,\mathrm{J/(mol\,K)}\). At \(360\,\mathrm K\) the enthalpy term in \(\ln(K_2/K_1)\) is \(-1.336\) and the heat-capacity term is \(+0.188\). Thus

\[K_2=4.00e^{-1.148}=1.27.\]

The association remains exothermic throughout the interval, although its magnitude declines on heating.

Second application

Infer enthalpy from equilibrium measurements

For a different reaction \(K\) rises from \(0.500\) at \(290\,\mathrm K\) to \(0.900\) at \(310\,\mathrm K\). If the reaction heat-capacity difference is negligible here, inversion gives

\[\Delta_rH^\circ=R\ln(0.900/0.500)/(1/290-1/310)=22.0\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}.\]

The positive sign is consistent with the increased equilibrium constant on heating. At \(300\,\mathrm K\) the same enthalpy predicts a local logarithmic slope of \(0.0293\,\mathrm{K^{-1}}\), testable with a more closely spaced measurement.

A reaction has one constrained direction

A closed vessel can change particle species while conserving the total number of atoms of each element. At fixed temperature and pressure the equilibrium state minimizes Gibbs energy. Introduce a reaction extent \(\xi\) in moles and stoichiometric coefficients \(\nu_i\), negative for reactants and positive for products. A small reaction advance changes amounts by \(dn_i=\nu_i\,d\xi\). The Gibbs differential at fixed \(T,p\) therefore gives

\[dG=\sum_i\mu_i\,dn_i=\Delta_r G\,d\xi,\]
\[\Delta_rG=\sum_i\nu_i\mu_i .\]

An interior minimum satisfies \(\Delta_rG=0\). A negative value means that a small positive advance lowers \(G\). Reversibility of the microscopic chemistry is assumed for equilibrium to be accessible. Thermodynamic preference alone does not provide the time needed to reach it.

Activities and the equilibrium constant

For ideal gases \(\mu_i=\mu_i^\circ(T)+RT\ln(p_i/p^\circ)\). The activity is the dimensionless ratio \(a_i=p_i/p^\circ\). Inserting this expression into the reaction Gibbs energy gives

\[\Delta_rG=\Delta_rG^\circ+RT\ln Q,\]

with \(Q=\prod_i a_i^{\nu_i}\). The equilibrium value of \(Q\) is \(K=\exp[-\Delta_rG^\circ/(RT)]\). Standard pressure supplies the reference that makes the logarithm and the equilibrium constant dimensionless even when the total molecular count changes.

For the dimerization \(2A\rightleftharpoons A_2\), begin with one mole of monomer units and define \(\alpha\) as the fraction of units bound into dimers. Then \(n_A=1-\alpha\), \(n_{A_2}=\alpha/2\) and total gas amount is \(1-\alpha/2\) moles on this basis. Partial pressures follow from mole fractions times total pressure. Substitution into the reaction quotient gives

\[Q=\frac{\alpha(2-\alpha)}{4(1-\alpha)^2}\frac{p^\circ}{p}.\]

The ratio of activities is determined by both composition and total pressure. Compression at the original equilibrium composition immediately lowers \(Q\), making the forward reaction favourable. The subsequent association reduces the number of gas particles while conserving monomer units.

A pressure change at fixed temperature

Suppose \(K=0.750\) at the chosen temperature. Let \(y=1-\alpha\). Because \(\alpha(2-\alpha)=1-y^2\), solving \(Q=K\) gives

\[y=[1+4Kp/p^\circ]^{-1/2}.\]

At \(p=p^\circ\) this gives \(\alpha=0.500\), with one half of all units bound and only one third of gas particles being dimers. At \(p=4p^\circ\) the bound-unit fraction is

\[1-1/\sqrt{13}=0.723.\]

The distinction between fractions of conserved units and fractions of gas molecules matters for interpreting a spectroscopic composition measurement.

A temperature change can also move equilibrium. Differentiating \(\ln K=-\Delta_rG^\circ/(RT)\) and using the Gibbs–Helmholtz relation gives

\[d\ln K/dT=\Delta_rH^\circ/(RT^2).\]

For an exothermic association increasing temperature decreases \(K\) locally. Pressure changes at fixed temperature leave \(K\) itself fixed under the same standard-state convention. It is the composition-dependent quotient that adjusts to the imposed mechanical conditions.

The distinction between a chemical potential per mole and one per particle is essential in this derivation. Here partial pressures were combined with \(R\) because the extent was measured in moles. Molecular statistical mechanics instead uses \(k_B\) with energies per molecule, but both conventions give the same dimensionless ratio of equilibrium activities. A useful numerical check is to scale every initial amount and the container volume by the same factor at fixed temperature. Mole fractions and partial pressures stay fixed, so the equilibrium fraction is unchanged even though twice as many molecules may react.

Use a membrane to turn chemical equilibrium into pressure

Equality of chemical potential can constrain a species even when other species cannot move. Separate pure solvent at pressure \(p\) from a dilute ideal solution at pressure \(p+\Pi\) by a membrane permeable only to solvent. Hold temperature fixed and assume a nearly incompressible solvent with approximately constant partial molar volume \(\bar v_w\). The solvent can exchange across the membrane; solute cannot. Its equilibrium condition is therefore equality of solvent chemical potentials, even though total pressures and solute concentrations differ.

For an ideal solution the solvent chemical potential relative to pure solvent at the same pressure changes by \(RT\ln x_w\), where \(x_w\) is the solvent mole fraction. Increasing pressure by \(\Pi\) raises the solvent chemical potential by \(\int_p^{p+\Pi}\bar v_w\,dp'\simeq\bar v_w\Pi\). Equating the two sides gives

\[\Pi=-\frac{RT}{\bar v_w}\ln x_w\simeq \frac{RT}{\bar v_w}x_s\simeq RT c_s .\]

The last approximation assumes a small solute mole fraction \(x_s\) and solution volume close to the solvent volume, with \(c_s\) in moles of independently dissolved particles per cubic metre. The pressure difference is positive because mixing lowers the chemical potential of solvent. If pressure is released, solvent flows into the solution, modifying its concentration until a new balance is attained.

Estimate a hydrostatic head and a molar mass

At 298 K dissolve 2.00 g/L of a nonvolatile solute with molar mass 0.200 kg/mol. The mass concentration is 2.00 kg/m³, so \(c_s=10.0\) mol/m³. Predicted osmotic pressure is \(8.314\times298\times10.0=24.8\) kPa. With solution density approximated by \(1000\) kg/m³, an open-column experiment would need height difference \(\Pi/(\rho g)=2.53\) m to balance it. The final concentration must be measured after the column rises, since transferred solvent can appreciably dilute a small sample.

Conversely, for the same 2.00 g/L preparation a pressure reading of 12.4 kPa would imply an apparent molar mass \(RT(2.00)/12400=0.400\) kg/mol. Association of two formula units into one particle is one possible explanation if the chemical analysis gives 0.200 kg/mol. Nonideal activities, leakage and concentration calibration can also change the inferred particle count. Repeating at lower concentrations tests whether \(\Pi/c_s\) approaches the ideal-gas constant times temperature. In the pure-solvent limit \(x_w\to1\) the chemical-potential difference vanishes so no osmotic pressure is required, despite the membrane still being present.

Concentration units can be a major source of error in this example. One mole per litre is a thousand moles per cubic metre, so the gas constant in joules per mole kelvin gives a pressure in pascals only after this conversion. For fully dissociated dilute electrolytes there may also be more than one independently mobile particle per formula unit. Conversely strong ion pairing or aggregation can reduce the count. Measuring a nonvolatile neutral reference solute of known molar mass in the same apparatus provides a way to test both the pressure scale and the effectiveness of the membrane.

A dilute nonideal gas can display almost ideal pressure while its particles strongly avoid one another at short distance. Connect a two-particle interaction to pressure, internal energy and a measurable pair correlation. Then use the resulting integral equations to ask which features of a potential can actually be inferred from a limited set of pressure readings.

Chapter 12 · Entropy production and relaxation

Derive a measurable rate of entropy production during contact between finite bodies and test it using temperature histories.

From first principles

Derive entropy production during heat exchange

Connect two bodies in a thermally isolated enclosure. Assume each body reaches internal equilibrium quickly enough to have a single temperature, and no external work is done. Let \(J>0\) denote energy flowing per time from the hot body at \(T_h\) to the cooler one at \(T_c\). Their internal energies change at equal and opposite rates. Using the equilibrium state relation \(dS_i=dU_i/T_i\) for each body at fixed volume and composition gives

\[\dot S_{\rm total}=-\frac{J}{T_h}+\frac{J}{T_c}=J\frac{T_h-T_c}{T_hT_c}.\]

This entropy production is positive while heat goes from hot to cold. To predict a relaxation time requires an empirical heat-flow relationship. If the contact has constant conductance \(G\), so \(J=G(T_h-T_c)\), and the heat capacities \(C_h,C_c\) stay constant, energy balance gives

\[\frac{d(T_h-T_c)}{dt}=-G\left(\frac1{C_h}+\frac1{C_c}\right)(T_h-T_c).\]

The temperature difference decays exponentially. The sign of the entropy change follows from thermodynamics, while the measured conductance controls how quickly equilibrium is reached.

Derivation and applications

Connect the recovery of a two-state population to entropy production

A system can return to equilibrium exponentially even when its entropy production has a more complicated time dependence. Consider many independent units with two internal configurations A and B in contact with one heat bath at fixed temperature \(T\). Each changes from A to B with rate \(k_+\) and back with rate \(k_-\), both positive and constant. Write \(p\) for the fraction in B. Conservation of population gives the net forward rate per unit and its stable fixed point,

\[\dot p=k_+(1-p)-k_-p=-(k_++k_-)(p-p_*),\]
\[p_*=\frac{k_+}{k_++k_-}.\]

The solution is

\[p(t)=p_*+[p(0)-p_*]\exp[-(k_++k_-)t].\]

To relate that motion to thermodynamics, suppose the rates obey detailed balance with the bath. For an independently mixed ensemble the excess free energy per unit relative to its equilibrium population is

\[F(p)-F(p_*)=k_BT\left[p\ln\frac{p}{p_*}+(1-p)\ln\frac{1-p}{1-p_*}\right].\]

This expression combines the change in the two-state energy average with the entropy of distributing the units between A and B. Differentiate with respect to \(p\), multiply by \(\dot p\), and use \(p_*/(1-p_*)=k_+/k_-\). Defining forward and reverse event rates \(j_+=k_+(1-p)\) and \(j_-=k_-p\) gives the entropy production per unit,

\[\dot S_{\rm total}=-\frac{\dot F}{T}=k_B(j_+-j_-)\ln(j_+/j_-)\geq0 .\]

The inequality follows because the larger positive flux also has the larger logarithm. At equilibrium the two one-way event rates can both be finite even though their difference and total entropy production vanish. Near equilibrium the thermodynamic driving force and net rate are both linear in \(p-p_*\), so their product decays twice as rapidly in its exponential time dependence.

Worked example

Compute the initial dissipation during recovery

Set \(k_+=3.00\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}\), \(k_-=1.00\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}\) and prepare \(p=0.250\). The forward and reverse rates are \(2.25\) and \(0.250\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}\). Initial entropy production is \(2.00\,k_B\ln9\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}=4.39\,k_B/\mathrm s\) per unit. After \(0.250\,\mathrm s\), one relaxation time, the population has risen to \(0.750-0.500/e=0.566\).

Second application

Infer microscopic rates from a relaxation trace

A different ensemble reaches equilibrium fraction \(p_*=0.200\). The magnitude of a small population offset halves every \(0.500\,\mathrm s\). The sum of the rates is \(\ln2/0.500=1.386\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}\); hence \(k_+=0.277\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}\) and \(k_-=1.109\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}\). At equilibrium each one-way flux is \(0.222\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}\) per unit. Event counting can test this prediction even when the mean population looks stationary.

Start from this chapter. Subtract the two energy balances to get an equation for the temperature difference. Use its exponential decay rate to decide which change of conductance or heat capacity can also change equilibrium.

OneSimulation laboratory · Separate the equilibrium temperature from the relaxation time

Two bodies with no external heat exchange

Connect two bodies through a weak thermal contact inside a perfectly insulated enclosure. Assume each equilibrates internally much faster than they exchange heat, so each has a single instantaneous temperature \(T_h\) or \(T_c\). Take their heat capacities \(C_h,C_c\) as positive constants over the range, with no work or phase change. Let \(J\) denote heat flowing per second from the initially hot body into the initially cold one. Energy conservation gives

\[C_h\dot T_h=-J,\]
\[C_c\dot T_c=J.\]

This immediately fixes the conserved weighted mean temperature.

A body's entropy change for this model depends only on its successive internal equilibrium states, so \(dS_i=C_i\,dT_i/T_i\). The bridge can carry irreversible heat while that state relation remains valid inside each nearly uniform body. Adding both entropy rates gives

\[\dot S_{\rm total}=J(1/T_c-1/T_h).\]

Positive heat flow down the temperature difference produces positive entropy. Equilibrium sets the thermodynamic force \(1/T_c-1/T_h\) to zero. Thermodynamics constrains the sign of \(J\), yet a constitutive heat-transfer law is still needed to predict how quickly temperatures change.

Identify a rate law experimentally

Suppose \(J=G(T_h-T_c)\) with temperature-independent thermal conductance \(G\). Subtracting the two temperature balances shows that \(\Delta=T_h-T_c\) satisfies

\[\dot\Delta=-G(1/C_h+1/C_c)\Delta.\]

The decaying difference and conserved weighted mean determine both temperature histories. The entropy-production rate becomes \(G\Delta^2/(T_hT_c)\). Near final temperature \(T_f\), the temperature difference decays exponentially while the entropy-production rate decays approximately twice as fast because it depends on the square.

The total entropy increase can also be obtained without integrating this rate. Integrating each state differential from its initial temperature to the common final value gives

\[\Delta S=C_h\ln(T_f/T_{h,0})+C_c\ln(T_f/T_{c,0}).\]

This expression is independent of conductance so long as the enclosure is isolated and the final state is the same. Larger conductance produces entropy faster at early times but shortens the duration of the process. Replacing a sliding-contact resistance by a smaller one changes the temperature record even when the equilibrium entropy gain is identical.

Predict a quantity beyond the equilibrium temperature

Take \(C_h=500\) J/K, \(C_c=1500\) J/K, \(T_{h,0}=360\) K, \(T_{c,0}=300\) K and \(G=2.00\) W/K. Conservation gives \(T_f=315\) K. The initial heat current is 120 W, and \(\dot S(0)=120(1/300-1/360)=0.0667\) W/K. The relaxation time is 187.5 s. The net entropy gain is \(500\ln(315/360)+1500\ln(315/300)=6.42\) J/K to two decimal places.

Use the two-body temperature histories to estimate the initial entropy-production rate and sum changes in \(C_i\ln T_i\) over the record. Doubling the conductance should double the initial rate and halve the measured relaxation time. Extending both runs to the same final tolerance should recover the same total entropy gain. A discrepancy that decreases as the sampling interval shrinks points to time resolution in the estimated initial slope.

At a finite recorded time the entropy increase is smaller than its asymptotic endpoint value. Evaluate the state-function expression at the last recorded temperatures before attributing a shortfall to the numerical algorithm. The remaining difference measures entropy still to be produced during subsequent equilibration.

Couple heat transport to electrical current

A thermal bridge can also carry electric charge. In a simple thermoelectric generator a temperature difference produces an electromotive force through the Seebeck effect, while current carries Peltier heat at each end. Take an idealized device with constant effective Seebeck coefficient \(S\), internal resistance \(R\), open-circuit thermal conductance \(K\) and no additional contact losses. Let \(T_h>T_c\) be externally fixed endpoint temperatures and choose positive current \(I\) as useful generator output. Connect a passive load \(R_L\) to the device.

The open-circuit voltage is \(S(T_h-T_c)\). Current through the load is \(I=S\Delta T/(R+R_L)\), giving useful power \(P=I^2R_L=IS\Delta T-I^2R\). For a uniform element with constant properties, half its internal Joule heat flows to each end. The reversible heat carried per unit charge is \(ST\) by the Kelvin relation. Combining these contributions with Fourier conduction gives hot-side input and cold-side output,

\[\dot Q_h=ST_hI+K\Delta T-\tfrac12I^2R,\]
\[\dot Q_c=ST_cI+K\Delta T+\tfrac12I^2R .\]

Their difference is exactly the electrical output. With the sign conventions fixed, the total reservoir entropy production is \(\dot Q_c/T_c-\dot Q_h/T_h\). The Peltier contributions cancel, leaving a positive term from conduction and another from Joule dissipation. This explicitly separates a reversible cross effect from two irreversible processes in the same device.

Find a matched-load operating point

Use \(T_h=350\) K, \(T_c=300\) K, \(S=200\) μV/K, \(R=0.100\) Ω and \(K=0.00200\) W/K. The open-circuit voltage is \(0.0100\) V. With matched load \(R_L=0.100\) Ω, current is \(0.0500\) A and useful power \(0.250\) mW. Conductive heat leakage alone is \(0.100\) W. At the hot end the Peltier contribution is 3.50 mW and half the internal Joule heating is 0.125 mW. Thus \(\dot Q_h=103.375\) mW and \(\dot Q_c=103.125\) mW. Their measured difference is much smaller than either heat current.

The operating efficiency \(P/\dot Q_h=0.00242\) is far below the reversible limit \(1-300/350=0.143\). Maximizing \(P=(S\Delta T)^2R_L/(R+R_L)^2\) at fixed endpoint temperatures indeed gives \(R_L=R\), but this choice need not maximize efficiency because the heat input also depends on current. With the circuit open the load receives zero power while \(K\Delta T\) still crosses the element and produces entropy. A reliable laboratory test therefore records electrical power and both thermal flows separately instead of interpreting an open-circuit voltage as evidence of appreciable useful energy conversion.

The numerical heat currents allow a direct entropy audit. The reservoirs together gain \(0.103125/300-0.103375/350=4.84\times10^{-5}\) W/K. Most of this is already explained by bare heat conduction, since \(0.100(1/300-1/350)=4.76\times10^{-5}\) W/K. The small remainder is the Joule contribution deposited at the two ends. This calculation uses reservoir rates with signs for heat leaving the hot bath and entering the cold bath. A sign error can suggest negative entropy production when the parameters instead describe an ordinary inefficient generator.

Recording the cold-end heat flow with its sign explicitly marked avoids the common confusion between heat entering the cold reservoir and heat entering the device.

Account for entropy during isolated thermal exchange

Two equal, temperature-independent heat capacities begin at 350 K and 250 K and exchange heat through a constant conductance. Energy fixes their common final temperature at 300 K. The temperature difference decays exponentially and each entropy change is \(C\ln(T/T_i)\).

A two-state detector can switch at random while displaying reproducible occupation fractions and relaxation times. Problem sheet 6 · Equilibrium, kinetics and irreversibility

Separate a chemical equilibrium constant from a thermal relaxation coefficient and quantify entropy changes in a finite system.

Change the gas volume

At fixed temperature an ideal dimerization \(2A\rightleftharpoons A_2\) has \(K=2.00\). At total pressure \(p^\circ\) find the bound-unit fraction and dimer mole fraction. Immediately expand isothermally until all original partial pressures have halved. Find the instantaneous reaction quotient and the preferred direction.

Show the composition and direction

With bound-unit fraction \(\alpha\), equilibrium gives

\[1-\alpha=(1+4Kp/p^\circ)^{-1/2}=1/3.\]

Hence \(\alpha=2/3\) and the dimer mole fraction \(\alpha/(2-\alpha)=1/2\). Because \(Q=a_{A_2}/a_A^2\), halving both partial pressures doubles \(Q\) from 2 to 4 before chemical readjustment. Thus \(\Delta_rG=RT\ln(Q/K)>0\), favouring dissociation. Continuing mechanical readjustment depends on whether volume or pressure is subsequently held fixed.

Two equal heat capacities

Two insulated blocks each have \(C=200\) J/K and start at 320 and 280 K. Find the common temperature, total entropy gain and initial entropy-production rate for conductance 1.50 W/K. What is their temperature difference after 50.0 s?

Show the balance and rate

The final temperature is 300 K. Entropy gain is

\[200\ln[300^2/(320\times280)]=0.891\,\mathrm{J/K}.\]

Initial current is \(1.50(40)=60.0\) W and initial entropy production is \(60(1/280-1/320)=0.0268\) W/K. With equal capacities \(\tau=C/(2G)=66.7\) s. The difference after 50.0 s is

\[40e^{-0.75}=18.9\,\mathrm{K}.\]

The final entropy gain depends only on endpoints, while initial rate and time history depend on conductance.

Determine whether a drift is heat leakage

A trace from two strongly insulated bodies has equal capacities of 150 J/K. Initially the measured temperatures are 330 and 290 K. After the difference has vanished both read 309 K. Estimate the apparent net heat exchange with the surroundings. Can increasing internal contact conductance explain it? Give an independent instrumental diagnosis.

Show the energy inventory

For equal capacities the initial arithmetic mean is 310 K and must stay fixed under pure internal heat exchange. Final readings imply \(\Delta U=150(309-330)+150(309-290)=-300\) J. Finite contact conductance can change the approach rate, but its internal current cancels in the total energy balance. A common thermometer drift of \(-1\) K between beginning and end would create the same apparent loss. Calibration against an independent temperature reference, or an enclosure heat-flux measurement, distinguishes these possibilities.

Extract work from a finite hot body

A body of constant heat capacity 1.00 kJ/K cools from 500 K to 300 K. A large reservoir stays at 300 K. Find the maximum work recoverable, the heat delivered to the reservoir and the entropy generated by direct thermal contact. Then predict how much of the available work remains if cooling stops at 400 K.

Worked solution

For a reversible sequence of small engines the instantaneous efficiency is 1 − T₀/T, where T is the body's current temperature. The body supplies −C dT on cooling, so Wₘₐₓ = C[(Tᵢ − T₀) − T₀ ln(Tᵢ/T₀)] = 46.75 kJ. Applying the initial Carnot efficiency to the entire 200 kJ would overestimate the work because the hot-side temperature falls.

The remaining 153.25 kJ enters the reservoir. Its entropy gain is 153.25/300 = 0.5108 kJ/K, equal to the magnitude of C ln(300/500) lost by the body. With direct contact, the reservoir instead receives all 200 kJ and total entropy production is 0.6667 − 0.5108 = 0.1558 kJ/K. Multiplication by 300 K recovers the 46.75 kJ of lost work.

At 400 K the body still has C[100 − 300 ln(4/3)] = 13.70 kJ available relative to the reservoir. The reversible work already extracted is therefore 33.05 kJ. Additivity of these two stages provides a check on both the logarithm and the choice of reference temperature.

Identify a heat capacity and a bridge conductance

Two insulated blocks start at 360 and 300 K. The cooler block has heat capacity 1500 J/K. The capacity-weighted equilibrium temperature is 320 K, and a fitted temperature difference decays by a factor \(e\) in 125 s. Infer the unknown hot-block heat capacity and the conductance. Predict the two observables after doubling that conductance in the downloadable model.

Work through the solution

Energy conservation gives \(C_h(360-320)=1500(320-300)\), hence \(C_h=750\) J/K. Subtracting the two block balances gives

\[1/\tau=G(1/C_h+1/C_c).\]

Therefore \(G=[125(1/750+1/1500)]^{-1}=4.00\) W/K. Doubling \(G\) to 8.00 W/K gives 62.5 s and leaves the final temperature at 320 K. Equilibrium data alone would identify the heat-capacity ratio while leaving the conductance undetermined.

Chapter 13 · How a finite heat bath changes a fluctuation

A tiny sample exchanges heat with its mounting plate inside an insulated chamber. A thermometer samples the same mean temperature whether the plate is large or small. Can the time record of the sample energy reveal the size of the plate?

Count the states compatible with one reading

Call the two bodies A and B. Fix total energy \(U\), volume and particle numbers. Assume weak thermal contact so energies add, although exchange occurs over the observation time. Divide energy into small equal bins wide enough to contain many microstates. If the sample has energy \(E\), the plate must have \(U-E\). Under the microcanonical equal-weight hypothesis the probability of this bin is proportional to the product of the two state counts. Introduce \(S=k_B\ln\Omega\). Maximising probability is now equivalent to maximising a sum.

\[k_B\ln P(E)=S_A(E)+S_B(U-E)+\text{constant}.\]

Moving energy from B to A increases the first entropy with slope \(1/T_A\) and decreases the second with slope \(1/T_B\). At an interior maximum their temperatures therefore agree. This argument determines the position of the peak. Its width requires one more derivative. At fixed volume \(dT/dE=1/C\), so differentiating \(1/T\) with respect to energy gives \(-1/(T^2 C)\). Differentiating the plate's entropy twice brings two factors of minus one from its argument. Its curvature consequently enters with the same sign as the sample curvature.

\[\ln\frac{P(E_*+\delta E)}{P(E_*)}\simeq-\frac{(\delta E)^2}{2k_BT^2}\left(\frac1{C_A}+\frac1{C_B}\right).\]

For positive heat capacities the peak is stable. Match this expression to the exponent of a Gaussian to identify \(\sigma_E^2=k_BT^2 C_A C_B/(C_A+C_B)\). The reciprocal capacities add because heating A also cools B. A genuinely macroscopic plate changes temperature so little that its reciprocal capacity disappears. The remaining formula then agrees with the canonical variance.

Background · Heat capacity
\[C_V=\operatorname{var}(E)/(k_BT^2)\]

This fluctuation formula uses a canonical equilibrium distribution at fixed volume and a temperature-independent energy operator. A finite reservoir suppresses subsystem fluctuations.

Two calorimeters at the same temperature

Measure energies in \(k_BT\) and capacities in \(k_B\). Let A have capacity 60. An effectively infinite reservoir gives a standard deviation \(\sqrt{60}=7.75\). A plate with equal capacity gives

\[\sqrt{30}=5.48.\]

A plate with capacity 20 gives

\[\sqrt{15}=3.87.\]

Doubling the width would quadruple the variance. These distinctions matter if an energy histogram is used to estimate heat capacity. In the equal-capacity case, applying the canonical formula would yield 30 instead of the actual 60.

A second consequence concerns correlations. Within this isolated system a fluctuation of \(+3k_BT\) in A forces a change of \(-3k_BT\) in B. Their covariance equals \(-\sigma_E^2\). The temperatures consequently fluctuate in opposite directions by amounts inversely proportional to each body's capacity. Repeated measurements must be spaced by the relaxation time if their scatter is to estimate an equilibrium variance with independent samples.

Compare two normalised histograms

Keep the sample capacity fixed while reducing the reservoir capacity. A narrower curve must grow taller to retain unit integrated probability. Locate the displacement at which its height is about 61 percent of its maximum. This displacement measures one standard deviation directly in the horizontal units. The quadratic expansion models the central peak. Energy bounds, strong coupling or a heat capacity varying substantially across the peak require the original entropy functions.

Tutorial on inferring a heat capacity

A sample with heat capacity \(90k_B\) has a measured standard deviation of \(6k_BT\). Infer the plate capacity and predict the scatter when the original plate is replaced with two identical plates in thermal contact.

Work through the solution

The measured variance in thermal units is 36. Write \(1/36=1/90+1/c_B\) to obtain \(c_B=60\). Two plates give 120. The new variance is \(90(120)/210=51.43\), so the standard deviation is \(7.17k_BT\). Increasing the plate capacity moves the result towards the canonical limit \(\sqrt{90}k_BT\).

A calorimeter measures both bodies simultaneously. Its inferred temperature deviations have slope \(\delta T_B/\delta T_A=-3\). Combined with an energy variance \(15(k_BT)^2\), determine both capacities.

Work through the solution

Energy conservation gives \(\delta T_B/\delta T_A=-C_A/C_B\), hence \(C_A=3C_B\). The effective dimensionless capacity is \(3c_B/4=15\). Thus \(C_B=20k_B\) and \(C_A=60k_B\). A covariance measurement and a histogram together identify both parameters where a width alone would give only their harmonic combination.

How would halving both heat capacities change their energy scatter and their temperature scatter at unchanged \(T\)?

Work through the solution

The effective capacity scales by one half, so \(\sigma_E\) decreases by \(1/\sqrt2\). Each temperature scatter is \(\sigma_E/C\) and increases by \(\sqrt2\). Smaller thermal systems can exhibit smaller absolute energy excursions and larger temperature excursions simultaneously.

Chapter 14 · Counting occupied sites on a surface

A surface with \(M\) identical sites exchanges particles with a gas. As the gas chemical potential rises, the coverage grows and eventually levels off. The same measurement also predicts the magnitude of number fluctuations, without estimating a time-dependent sticking rate.

Start with one site and a reservoir

An empty site has energy zero and population zero. An occupied site has energy \(-\epsilon\) with \(\epsilon>0\), and population one. Assume each site can bind at most one particle, the sites do not interact, and both states have unit degeneracy. A reservoir that supplies heat and particles assigns a state weight proportional to \(\exp[-\beta(E-\mu N)]\), where \(\beta=1/(k_BT)\). One may recover the combination \(E-\mu N\) by expanding the reservoir entropy after removing energy \(E\) and particles \(N\), using \(T\,dS=dU-\mu\,dN\) at fixed volume.

\[\Xi_1=1+e^{\beta(\mu+\epsilon)},\]
\[\theta=P(1)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-\beta(\mu+\epsilon)}}.\]

At \(\mu=-\epsilon\) empty and occupied are equally likely. A more negative chemical potential penalises bringing a particle out of the gas. Positive binding energy counteracts that penalty. The reference for both energies must be the same. For an ideal dilute gas at fixed temperature, changing the pressure from \(p_1\) to \(p_2\) changes the chemical potential by \(k_BT\ln(p_2/p_1)\). Thus doubling the pressure doubles the odds \(\theta/(1-\theta)\), even when the coverage itself grows only slightly.

Factorisation explains the noise

With independent sites every configuration has a product of one-site weights, so summing over all binary choices gives

\[\Xi=\Xi_1^M.\]

Alternatively group configurations by population \(N\). There are \(\binom{M}{N}\) ways to choose the occupied sites. Division by \(\Xi\) gives the binomial probability \(P(N)=\binom{M}{N}\theta^N(1-\theta)^{M-N}\). Since a binary variable satisfies \(n^2=n\), its variance is \(\theta-\theta^2\). Independent sites have zero cross-covariance. Adding their variances gives

\[\langle N\rangle=M\theta,\]
\[\operatorname{var}N=M\theta(1-\theta)=k_BT\left(\frac{\partial\langle N\rangle}{\partial\mu}\right)_T.\]

For \(M=100\) at half coverage the mean is 50 and the standard deviation is 5 particles. Raising the odds to 9 gives mean 90 and deviation 3. On the steep part of the isotherm small changes of reservoir conditions produce the largest response. Thermal noise is largest there for precisely the same reason. A broad distribution near a sharp steepening can also signal collective behaviour, but the independent-site prediction provides a quantitative comparison before invoking interactions.

Measure a shift in binding energy

Imagine comparing two surfaces in the same chamber. Their temperature and chemical potential agree. If the second binds particles more strongly by \(k_BT\ln4\), it multiplies the odds by four. Where the first has coverage \(1/5\), its odds are \(1/4\), so the second reaches exactly one half. Move the binding-energy slider and identify the chemical potential at the centre of the curve. The plot also displays the number variance per site on the same dimensionless scale. At very small coverage the two curves nearly coincide because \(\theta^2\) becomes negligible.

Tutorial on recovering an isotherm

At pressure \(p_0\) a surface has mean coverage 0.75. How much must pressure change for coverage 0.90 at the same temperature? For 400 sites, calculate the initial and final root-mean-square fluctuations in coverage.

Work through the solution

The odds change from 3 to 9, requiring \(p=3p_0\). The variance of the fractional coverage \(N/M\) is \(\theta(1-\theta)/M\). Taking square roots gives 0.0217 initially and 0.0150 finally. These numbers measure instantaneous equilibrium fluctuations. The uncertainty of a time average additionally depends on how long successive readings remain correlated.

Infer two independent predictions from the probability of a completely empty three-site patch at half coverage. What fraction of frames show at least two occupied sites?

Work through the solution

Empty probability is

\[(1/2)^3=1/8.\]

Two occupied sites have probability \(\binom32/8=3/8\), and three have probability \(1/8\), giving one half for at least two. Non-binomial counts at fixed mean are a direct test of equivalence and independence of the sites.

Suppose every occupied site admits two internal states of equal energy while an empty site has only one. Determine the shift of the half-coverage chemical potential.

Work through the solution

The one-site grand sum becomes \(1+2e^{\beta(\mu+\epsilon)}\). Half coverage requires the occupied and empty weights to agree, so \(\mu=-\epsilon-k_BT\ln2\). Internal entropy shifts the measured midpoint without changing the exclusion of a second particle.

Chapter 15 · How a pair potential changes the gas pressure

A low-density gas can measure its own intermolecular forces. At a prescribed temperature the first deviation from ideal behaviour is a volume. Its sign tells us whether overlap exclusion or attraction makes the larger contribution.

Separate independent pairs from correlated pairs

Let \(N\) classical particles occupy volume \(V\), with a total potential energy equal to a sum of short-range pair potentials \(u(r_{ij})\). Momentum integrals give the ideal-gas factors. In the remaining positional integral write each pair's Boltzmann weight as \(e^{-\beta u}=1+f(r)\). The auxiliary function \(f=e^{-\beta u}-1\) vanishes where particles do not interact. In a large vessel the positional integral with one \(f\) is \(V^{N-1}\int f(\boldsymbol r)\,d^3r\). One particle of the pair may be placed anywhere and its neighbour's relative coordinate is sampled against \(f\). There are \(N(N-1)/2\) possible unordered pairs.

In the low-density expansion of \(\ln Z\), independent repetitions of separate pairs cancel against products from the logarithm. The first connected correction is \(N(N-1)\int f/(2V)\). This is a density expansion of the free energy per particle. The total correction need not be small for a macroscopic sample. Differentiating with \(p=k_BT(\partial\ln Z/\partial V)_{T,N}\) supplies a minus sign from the reciprocal volume. In the thermodynamic limit with number density \(\rho=N/V\),

\[\frac{p}{\rho k_BT}=1+B_2(T)\rho+O(\rho^2),\]
\[B_2=-\tfrac12\int f\,d^3r=-2\pi\int_0^\infty f(r)r^2\,dr.\]

An impenetrable core gives \(f=-1\). An attractive annulus gives \(f>0\). The sign of \(B_2\) follows from their integrated volumes, including the spherical shell factor \(r^2\).

Integrate a square well

Set \(u=\infty\) for \(r<d\), \(u=-\epsilon\) for \(d<r<\lambda d\), and \(u=0\) outside. The two nonzero contributions are constants integrated over spherical volumes. With \(B_{\rm core}=2\pi d^3/3\), obtain

\[B_2=B_{\rm core}\{1-(\lambda^3-1)[e^{\epsilon/(k_BT)}-1]\}.\]

A sphere of diameter \(d\) has actual volume \(\pi d^3/6\). The hard-core coefficient is four times that volume. The forbidden positions concern the centre of a second particle, and the factor of one half avoids counting an interacting pair twice. For \(\lambda=1.5\) and \(k_BT/\epsilon=2\), the ratio \(B_2/B_{\rm core}=1-2.375(e^{0.5}-1)\simeq-0.541\). A dilute sample with \(\rho B_{\rm core}=0.02\) consequently has \(p/(\rho k_BT)\simeq0.9892\) at this order.

Locate the temperature at which the slope vanishes

Set \(B_2=0\) and solve for the Boyle temperature. The result is \(k_BT_B/\epsilon=1/\ln[1+1/(\lambda^3-1)]\), or 2.846 for the preceding range. Vary the width of the well. A larger attraction volume can offset the hard core even when the temperature is high. At \(T_B\) the pressure curve has zero first density correction. Three-particle contributions can still produce curvature. At very low temperatures pair binding can become strong enough that even a superficially low density fails to justify truncation.

Open this experiment and change its inputs online

Tutorial on inferring the range

In a square-well model the measured Boyle temperature is

\[k_BT_B/\epsilon=2.\]

Determine \(\lambda\), then predict the sign of the pressure correction when the temperature is doubled.

Work through the solution

Rearrangement gives \(\lambda^3=1+1/(e^{1/2}-1)=2.5415\), hence \(\lambda\simeq1.365\). Doubling the temperature decreases the attractive Boltzmann factor and leaves the hard-core term fixed. Substitution at reduced temperature 4 gives

\[B_2/B_{\rm core}\simeq1-1.5415(0.2840)=0.562.\]

At sufficiently low density the pressure exceeds the ideal prediction.

Can a negative \(B_2\) at one temperature fix how much of the molecular attraction comes from its depth and how much from its range?

Work through the solution

The coefficient in the square-well model depends on the product \((\lambda^3-1)[e^{\epsilon/k_BT}-1]\). Many combinations of width and depth give the same product. Measurements at two temperatures can constrain both parameters if the core diameter is independently known and the model is appropriate. Additional temperatures expose inadequacies in the assumed well shape.

Take two measured compressibility factors \(Z=0.9950,0.9900\) at \(\rho B_{\rm core}=0.010,0.020\) at the same temperature. Estimate \(B_2/B_{\rm core}\) and check consistency of the truncation with these two measurements.

Work through the solution

The slopes from the ideal limit are \((Z-1)/(\rho B_{\rm core})=-0.50\) for both points. Their common value agrees with a leading pair correction and shows no detectable curvature at the stated precision. It provides no bound on higher-order terms outside that measured density interval.

Further reading · Cambridge statistical physics, classical gases and the cluster expansion.

Chapter 16 · Why two coexisting phases share a tangent

A material prepared with an intermediate composition can separate into two regions of different compositions. Its total composition is conserved. How can a free-energy graph predict both final compositions and the amount of each phase?

Minimise the free energy of a mixture

Work at fixed temperature and volume with a constant density of equivalent sites. Let \(f(c)\) be the Helmholtz free energy per site of a spatially uniform state with fraction \(c\) of species B. If the two regions have compositions \(c_1,c_2\) and the second contains fraction \(x\) of all sites, conservation requires

\[\bar c=(1-x)c_1+xc_2.\]

Neglect interface energy per site in the macroscopic limit. The mixture free energy per site is then the weighted sum of the two \(f\)'s, a point on the chord joining them.

Introduce a multiplier \(\mu\) and minimise \((1-x)f(c_1)+xf(c_2)-\mu[(1-x)c_1+xc_2-\bar c]\). Varying \(c_1,c_2\) when both regions are present gives

\[f'(c_1)=f'(c_2)=\mu.\]

This derivative measures the chemical work to replace an A particle by B. Varying \(x\) supplies the missing condition,

\[f(c_2)-f(c_1)=\mu(c_2-c_1).\]

The common slope therefore equals the slope of the connecting chord. A straight line must touch the free energy at both endpoints and lie below competing homogeneous states. Equivalently \(\int_{c_1}^{c_2}[f'(c)-\mu]\,dc=0\). This equal-area condition is the composition version of Maxwell's construction. For liquids plotted as pressure versus specific volume, the conjugate slope acquires the sign from \(p=-\partial F/\partial V\).

Find the coexistence and stability boundaries separately

Take \(f(c)=A[(c-m)^2-d^2]^2+\mu_0c\), with \(A>0\), \(m=0.5\) and \(0<d<0.5\). Subtracting the linear term tilts all trial chords by the same amount. At \(c=m\pm d\) the remaining term vanishes with zero derivative. Hence the common tangent is \(\mu_0 c\), and the coexistence compositions are \(m-d,m+d\). At \(d=0.30\) a sample of average composition 0.45 separates into 0.20 and 0.80 regions. Conservation gives \(x=(0.45-0.20)/(0.80-0.20)=5/12\) for the B-rich region.

Now perturb a uniform state into two equal parts at \(c\pm\eta\). Their average energy differs from the uniform energy by \(f''(c)\eta^2/2+O(\eta^4)\). Here \(f''=4A[3(c-m)^2-d^2]\). Between \(m-d/\sqrt3\) and \(m+d/\sqrt3\) infinitesimal fluctuations reduce the energy. Between either of these limits and the nearest coexistence endpoint a uniform state resists small fluctuations but a sufficiently large rearrangement can still lower the energy. This accounts for metastability and for the distinction between spinodal and coexistence boundaries. The uniform model does not predict a nucleation time because interfaces carry no energy in this construction.

Get a phase fraction from a graph

The display subtracts \(\mu_0c\) and measures energies in \(A\). Move the mean composition across the whole interval. Outside the coexistence window the stable composition is homogeneous. Inside, the endpoints stay put while the rich-region fraction changes linearly. Compare \(c=0.45\) to \(c=0.55\) for the same gap. Reflection symmetry exchanges the two phase fractions and leaves the free-energy saving unchanged.

Open this experiment and change its inputs online

Tutorial on a composition quench

A homogeneous sample is prepared at \(c=0.26\) with \(d=0.30\). Does an infinitesimal composition fluctuation lower its energy? What fraction of the final mixture occupies the B-rich phase in equilibrium?

Work through the solution

The lower spinodal lies at \(0.5-0.3/\sqrt3=0.327\), so the prepared state lies below it and has positive curvature. Nevertheless 0.26 lies between 0.20 and 0.80. Its equilibrium rich fraction is

\[0.06/0.60=0.10.\]

Local stability and the global free-energy minimum answer different experimental questions.

For \(m=0.50\), \(d=0.30\), compare free-energy gains of demixing at mean compositions 0.20 and 0.50 after subtracting the tilt. Report the gain in units of \(A\).

Work through the solution

At a coexistence endpoint the pure homogeneous material already lies on the common tangent and has zero gain. At the midpoint the homogeneous energy exceeds the tangent by \(d^4 A=0.0081A\) per site. The equilibrium mixture uses equal amounts of the two compositions. The gain tends continuously to zero at either endpoint.

Would adding \(b+mc\) to the free energy change the two selected compositions or spinodals? What would change in the tangent construction?

Work through the solution

Conservation fixes the mean composition, so the new term contributes \(b+m\bar c\) to every candidate mixture at that mean. The minimiser is unchanged. Second derivatives are unchanged, preserving spinodals. Both endpoint tangent slopes, and thus the chemical-potential difference assigned to coexistence, shift by \(m\).

Further reading · Cambridge statistical physics, phase equilibrium and Maxwell construction.

Chapter 17 · Extracting a length from thermal spin fluctuations

A one-dimensional row of magnetic moments favours local alignment. At low temperature a snapshot can contain a long row of identical spins. An exact calculation distinguishes a large correlated domain from a thermodynamic phase with permanent order.

Sum all configurations by multiplying a small matrix

Consider \(N\) classical spins \(s_j=\pm1\) on a ring with \(s_{N+1}=s_1\). At zero applied field the energy is \(-J\sum_j s_js_{j+1}\) with \(J>0\). The Boltzmann weight factors into nearest-neighbour terms \(e^{Ks_js_{j+1}}\), with \(K=J/(k_BT)\). Construct the matrix \(T_{ss'}=e^{Kss'}\), whose diagonal elements are \(e^K\) and off-diagonal elements \(e^{-K}\). Multiplying \(T\)'s automatically sums each intermediate spin over its two choices. Closing the first and last indices gives

\[Z_N=\operatorname{tr}(T^N).\]

The symmetric and antisymmetric vectors \((1,1)/\sqrt2\) and \((1,-1)/\sqrt2\) have eigenvalues \(\lambda_+=2\cosh K\) and \(\lambda_-=2\sinh K\). Thus \(Z_N=\lambda_+^N+\lambda_-^N\). At every finite positive temperature the ratio of eigenvalues is strictly below one. In the large-system limit the free energy per spin is \(-k_BT\ln(2\cosh K)\). Differentiating with respect to \(\beta\) yields the energy per spin \(-J\tanh K\).

Background · Connected correlation
\[C(r)=\langle s_i s_{i+r}\rangle-\langle s_i\rangle\langle s_{i+r}\rangle\]

Subtract the independent contribution before identifying a decay length. A periodic sample introduces a second propagation distance around the ring.

Insert two local measurements

Multiplying an individual configuration by a measured spin corresponds to inserting \(S=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)\) in the matrix trace. To measure two sites separated by \(r\) bonds use \(\operatorname{tr}(ST^rST^{N-r})/Z_N\). In the eigenbasis of \(T\), \(S\) exchanges the symmetric and antisymmetric vectors. The numerator therefore contains one factor \(\lambda_-^r\lambda_+^{N-r}\) and one with the eigenvalues exchanged. With \(q=\lambda_-/\lambda_+=\tanh K\),

\[\langle s_0s_r\rangle_N=\frac{q^r+q^{N-r}}{1+q^N},\]
\[\langle s_0s_r\rangle_\infty=q^r=e^{-ra/\xi},\]
\[\xi=-\frac{a}{\ln q}.\]

Here \(a\) is the lattice spacing and the infinite-chain limit holds for fixed \(r\). The second finite-ring term comes from the other way around the circle. At equal sites the full ratio equals one. In zero field spin reversal makes the mean spin zero in the thermal distribution. Thus this correlation already equals the connected correlation.

Compare a chain at two temperatures

At \(k_BT=J\), \(q=0.7616\) and \(\xi=3.67a\). Spins ten bonds apart have correlation only \(0.0657\). At \(k_BT=0.5J\), \(\xi=27.30a\) and the corresponding correlation is \(0.693\). Lower temperature suppresses individual domain walls. Since \(s_js_{j+1}\) is +1 for alignment and −1 for a wall, its average equals \(1-2P_{\rm wall}=q\). At low temperature \(P_{\rm wall}\simeq e^{-2K}\) and \(\xi/a\simeq e^{2K}/2\). Even rare walls eventually destroy alignment in a sufficiently long chain.

Compare the finite ring with the infinite-chain result. Change the ring length while leaving the temperature fixed. When the correlation length becomes comparable to the circumference, the long route contributes appreciably. Returning to the starting site must restore correlation one. A straight-line fit to the back half of a semilog finite-ring plot would consequently give a misleading decay length.

Tutorial on estimating an interaction

In a very long zero-field chain the nearest-neighbour correlation is 0.6. Determine \(J/(k_BT)\), the probability of a wall on a given bond and the separation at which correlation first falls below 0.1.

Work through the solution

Invert \(q=\tanh K\) to obtain

\[K=\tfrac12\ln[(1+q)/(1-q)]=0.6931.\]

The wall probability is

\[(1-q)/2=0.20.\]

Solve \(r>\ln(0.1)/\ln(0.6)=4.51\). At five bonds the correlation is 0.07776. An even number of walls can restore the original spin direction, so this correlation counts more than the probability of finding a completely wall-free interval.

At \(k_BT=J\) a nearest-neighbour bond is aligned with probability \(p\). Find \(p\) and its relation to the mean energy per bond.

Work through the solution

The correlation is \(2p-1=\tanh1=0.7616\), so \(p=0.8808\). Multiplying \(2p-1\) by \(-J\) gives \(-0.7616J\). This directly connects counts of local defects in snapshots with the thermodynamic energy obtained from the partition function.

Why can an odd number of walls never occur on a closed ring? Would dropping the finite-ring correction give the correct wall count at arbitrary temperature?

Work through the solution

Each wall reverses the spin when following the ring. Returning to the starting site requires an even number of reversals. The exact nearest-neighbour correlation is \((q+q^{N-1})/(1+q^N)\). Thus the mean wall count is \(N(1-C_1)/2\). Approximating \(C_1\) by \(q\) works when \(N\) substantially exceeds the correlation length; otherwise ring closure changes the result.

Chapter 18 · Why only a narrow shell of a Fermi gas carries heat

Heating a filled Fermi sea does not give every particle a classical thermal energy. Deep below the chemical potential, nearby states are already occupied. Quantifying the accessible states predicts both the low-temperature heat capacity and the shift of the chemical potential at fixed particle number.

Convert a sharp Fermi surface into a narrow weight

For independent fermions with occupancy \(f(E)=1/[1+\exp((E-\mu)/(k_BT))]\), consider integrals \(I=\int_0^\infty H(E)f(E)\,dE\). Choose \(F(E)=\int_0^E H(s)ds\). Integration by parts gives \(I=\int_0^\infty F(E)[-\partial_E f(E)]dE\), since the boundary terms vanish. The derivative is a peak of width \(k_BT\) around \(\mu\). With \(x=(E-\mu)/(k_BT)\) the weight becomes

\[w(x)=1/[4\cosh^2(x/2)].\]

For \(\mu\) many thermal units above the bottom and \(H\) smooth over the thermal shell, extend the lower limit to \(-\infty\) when expanding locally around \(\mu\). The weight has unit integral and is even, so the linear term in \(F(\mu+k_BTx)\) integrates to zero. Its second moment is \(\pi^2/3\), obtained by expanding \(w(x)=\sum_{\ell\ge1}(-1)^{\ell+1}\ell e^{-\ell x}\) on \(x>0\) and integrating \(x^2\) termwise. Since \(F''=H'\),

\[I=\int_0^\mu H(E)dE+\frac{\pi^2}{6}(k_BT)^2H'(\mu)+O(T^4).\]

The first correction samples the slope of the smooth weighting function. If a band edge or singularity lies within the shell, replacing the lower limit and Taylor expanding are poor approximations.

Conserve the number of particles

For a three-dimensional parabolic dispersion the density of states is \(D(E)=A\sqrt E\). At \(T=0\), \(N=(2A/3)E_F^{3/2}\). At small \(T\), use the expansion with \(H=D\) and write the chemical potential as \(E_F+\delta\mu\), where \(\delta\mu=O(T^2)\). Subtract the zero-temperature count. To quadratic order \(0=D(E_F)\delta\mu+(\pi^2/6)(k_BT)^2D'(E_F)\). Because \(D'/D=1/(2E_F)\),

\[\mu/E_F=1-\frac{\pi^2}{12}(T/T_F)^2+O[(T/T_F)^4],\]
\[T_F=E_F/k_B.\]

The increasing density of states offers more available levels just above the Fermi energy than just below it. The chemical potential shifts down to preserve the count. At \(T/T_F=0.10\) the predicted shift is \(-0.00822E_F\). For an ideal gas with \(E_F=5.0\,\mathrm{eV}\), this particular reduced temperature corresponds to about 5800 K, so reduced temperature and ordinary laboratory temperature should be distinguished.

Differentiate the energy at fixed number

Use \(H=ED\) in the same integral, including the just-derived shift of \(\mu\). The boundary shift contributes \(E_FD(E_F)\delta\mu\). In the Sommerfeld term the derivative is \(D(E_F)+E_FD'(E_F)\). The terms involving the slope of \(D\) cancel after fixing number. Thus \(U-U_0=(\pi^2/6)D(E_F)(k_BT)^2\), and \(C_V=(\pi^2/3)D(E_F)k_B^2T\). In three dimensions \(D(E_F)=3N/(2E_F)\), giving \(C_V/(Nk_B)=(\pi^2/2)T/T_F\). This is an electronic contribution for independent particles. Other degrees of freedom such as phonons can dominate a measured material heat capacity.

The experiment reconstructs \(\mu\) by numerical integration and bisection at fixed number. It overlays the asymptotic prediction, allowing the fractional error to be checked before using it at larger \(T/T_F\). The quadrature uses the momentum-like substitution \(E/E_F=y^2\) to remove the square-root endpoint singularity.

For a gas with \(E_F=4.0\,\mathrm{eV}\) at \(T=300\,\mathrm K\), estimate \(C_V/(Nk_B)\) and the chemical-potential change in eV. Use \(k_BT=0.02585\,\mathrm{eV}\).

Work through the solution

The reduced temperature is \(0.00646\). The heat capacity ratio is approximately \(0.0319\), and \(\delta\mu=-(\pi^2/12)(0.02585)^2/4.0=-1.37\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{eV}\).

A two-dimensional parabolic band has constant density of states above its edge. What does the quadratic expansion predict for the fixed-number chemical potential and energy?

Work through the solution

\(D'=0\) makes the quadratic shift of \(\mu\) vanish as long as the edge is distant. The energy integral still uses \((ED)'=D\), so it has a positive \(T^2\) correction. Effects of the distant band edge can give exponentially small departures in \(\mu\).

Chapter 19 · Mean-field ordering, response and the critical point

Interactions can make a magnet favour a nonzero moment even when the applied field vanishes. Averaging the local exchange field gives a solvable model whose critical predictions can be compared with the exact one-dimensional chain.

Build the free energy from the count of spin states

Take \(N\) spins \(s_i=\pm1\), nearest-neighbour energy \(-J\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}s_is_j\) and Zeeman energy \(-h\sum_i s_i\), where \(h\) has energy units. Denote mean spin by \(m\). The fractions of positive and negative spins are \(p_\pm=(1\pm m)/2\). The binomial count and Stirling's approximation give entropy per spin \(-k_B(p_+\ln p_++p_-\ln p_-)\). Independent-neighbour mean field replaces each pair average by \(m^2\). With \(z\) neighbours and each bond counted once, interaction energy per spin becomes \(-zJm^2/2\).

\[f(m)=-\tfrac12zJm^2-hm+k_BT[p_+\ln p_++p_-\ln p_-].\]

Differentiate at fixed \(T,h\). The entropy contribution has derivative \(k_BT\operatorname{atanh}m\), giving \(m=\tanh[(zJm+h)/(k_BT)]\). This equation can have three real roots, so an iterative solver returning a root alone is insufficient. The equilibrium phase minimises \(f\); the second derivative \(k_BT/(1-m^2)-zJ\) distinguishes local minima and maxima.

Expand about the loss of stability

Near zero magnetisation,

\[\operatorname{atanh}m=m+m^3/3+\cdots.\]

Set \(T_c=zJ/k_B\) and integrate the expanded derivative to obtain

\[f(m)-f(0)\simeq\tfrac{k_B}{2}(T-T_c)m^2+\tfrac{k_BT}{12}m^4-hm .\]

At zero field and \(T>T_c\), \(m=0\) is stable. Below \(T_c\), symmetry gives two minima whose leading magnitudes satisfy \(m^2\simeq3(T_c-T)/T\). Thus the order parameter vanishes like \((T_c-T)^{1/2}\) close to \(T_c\). At \(T=T_c\) a small nonzero field instead gives

\[m\simeq[3h/(k_BT_c)]^{1/3}.\]

These powers describe this model's limiting behaviour. For a finite sample symmetry makes the unbiased ensemble average zero if it samples both minima. Spontaneous magnetisation refers to the thermodynamic limit with an infinitesimal field selecting a sign.

Compute a response, then compare with an exact counterexample

Above \(T_c\) the small-field stationary equation gives

\[\chi=\partial m/\partial h=1/[k_B(T-T_c)].\]

Below \(T_c\), differentiate the exact stationarity equation on the positive branch, obtaining \(\chi=[k_BT/(1-m^2)-zJ]^{-1}\). Expanding near \(T_c\) there gives \(\chi\simeq[2k_B(T_c-T)]^{-1}\), half the above-transition amplitude at equal distance. At \(T=0.8T_c\), the full zero-field solution is about \(m=0.7104\); the small-\(m\) estimate \(\sqrt{3(1-0.8)/0.8}=0.866\) is already visibly inaccurate.

Mean field predicts an ordering temperature even for a one-dimensional chain with \(z=2\). The exact finite-temperature correlation length in the earlier transfer-matrix solution is finite at all \(T>0\). Spatial fluctuations and domain walls invalidate the independent-neighbour closure in one dimension. The experiment plots the full mean-field free energy and its quartic approximation for the same normalised \(T,h\). Find the minima before inspecting the calculated order parameter. Compare how a weak bias changes their relative depths.

Tutorial on critical response

At \(T=1.10T_c\), what is the linear-response mean spin expected at \(h/(k_BT_c)=0.002\)? At the critical point use the cubic equation to estimate \(m\) for the same field.

Work through the solution

Above the transition \(m\simeq0.002/0.10=0.020\). At criticality \(m\simeq(0.006)^{1/3}=0.182\). The larger response signals the loss of the quadratic restoring term; linear extrapolation through \(T_c\) would give a divergent susceptibility.

At \(h=0\) and \(T=0.95T_c\), is \(m=0\) a possible output from a fixed-point solver? How should an equilibrium calculation prevent a wrong interpretation?

Work through the solution

Starting the symmetric iteration at exactly zero returns zero repeatedly, even below \(T_c\). Its free-energy curvature is \(k_B(T-T_c)<0\); it is a local maximum. Compare the free energies or bracket the two symmetry-related nonzero stationary points before reporting an equilibrium moment.
